Tea was first planted in Kenya in 1903 at Limuru, near Nairobi, and grew into one of the country's main exports, making Kenya the world's largest exporter of black tea.

Under colonial rule, large estates owned by British firms grew most of it around Kericho in the western highlands. Africans were long barred from growing it. After independence, a state agency helped hundreds of thousands of smallholders take up the crop, and they now grow most of Kenya's tea.

The tea, mostly sold at the Mombasa auction, goes into tea bags in Britain, Pakistan, Egypt and elsewhere. It shaped the highlands as much as the settler farms did, and is part of the long tea trade of the British Empire. It is a pillar of Kenya's economy.
